title: Keeping the pace
hookLine: the meters quicken like drums; many recite Jaap briskly, as marching music for the spirit
last: KAAL — DEATH IS IN HIS HAND.

lines: DRUMS BEFORE YOU SEE THE BAND.
cards: The marching band is still two streets away, and already your shoulders have gone back. Your step falls into time without permission. The kids on the curb start stomping, and a grandmother on a bench taps her cane.
Nobody decided to keep the beat; the beat picked them up and carried them. That's what a steady rhythm does to a body. Tired legs keep going, and a wandering mind stays in line.

teach.h: GLIDE, STEPS, TINY LINES, ONE LETTER.
teach.b: Over three weeks you've heard Jaap change its walk again and again: the snake's long glide of bhujang prayat, the quick two-word steps of chachari, the tiny lines of harbolmana, and the one-letter meter, ek achhari, where the words shrink to almost nothing.

teach.h: THE PACE QUICKENS LIKE A DRUMMER.
teach.b: Listen to them in order, and as the hymn goes on, many of the lines get shorter and the pace quicker, like a drummer speeding up toward the end of a song.
That's why many Sikhs recite Jaap briskly, not slowly and solemnly. Ask around and you'll hear it called marching music for the spirit.

It has what Indian poetics calls bir ras, the heroic mood, the feeling of standing tall and moving forward. It fits the Guru who wrote it, a poet and a leader of soldiers at once. But the speed isn't only about courage.
It's also about attention. Recite slowly, and the mind has time to wander off to lunch.

teach.h: AT PACE, NO ROOM TO WANDER.
teach.b: At pace, there's no room: each line arrives right behind the last, and you have to stay with it.
The praise carries you, the way the drums carry a tired marcher. It's the same idea as day three hundred thirty-two, praise at pace, now heard from the inside.

how: Many Sikhs recite Jaap Sahib briskly from memory each morning, letting its quickening meters carry them, and in a gurdwara a whole sangat may recite it together at speed.

o: a drum that keeps time for marchers
a short hymn sung at the end of prayers
a meter, the beat a hymn's lines walk in

games.q: keeping the pace — tap the pairs.

s: Jaap is usually recited slowly and solemnly
many Sikhs recite it briskly, as marching music for the spirit.
as Jaap goes on, many of its lines get shorter
from the long glide to two-word steps to the one-letter meter.
bir ras is the name of one of Jaap's meters
bir ras is the heroic mood of Indian poetics; the meters have names like bhujang prayat and chachari.

games.q: you're reciting Jaap and your mind keeps drifting to lunch. what does reciting at pace do?
o: leaves no room to wander: each line arrives right behind the last.
games.why: the speed is about attention as well as courage: the praise carries you, the way drums carry a tired marcher.

practice: Tap your knee for the beat and say ten lines you already know, once slowly to find them: namastvam akaale, namastvam kripaale, namastvam aroope, namastvam anoope, aroop hain, anoop hain, ajoo hain, abhoo hain, karunaalay hain, khal khanddan hain.
Then say them once more at pace, without stopping, and feel your back straighten. Sit still and let the beat fade.

wordCard.voice: Chhand. A meter — Jaap moves through around ten of them, quickening like drums, so many Sikhs recite it briskly, as marching music for the spirit.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: chhand, a meter; Jaap moves through around ten of them, quickening as it goes.

carryVoice: Your line: march in praise. At pace, there's no room to wander. Day three hundred fifty-five, done.
